quote: For building muscle mass and for maintaining muscle mass through a positive muscle protein balance, an overall daily protein intake in the range of 1.4–2.0 g protein/kg body weight/day (g/kg/d) is sufficient for most exercising individuals
claim: ISSN: a daily protein intake of 1.4-2.0 g/kg body weight is sufficient for most exercising people to build and maintain muscle.

quote: Recommendations for protein intake typically range from 1.2 to 2.0 g/kg BW/d, but have more recently been expressed in terms of the regular spacing of intakes of modest amounts of high quality protein (0.3 g/kg BW) after exercise and throughout the day. Such intakes can generally be met from food sources.
claim: ACSM/AND/DC: athletes' protein needs are typically 1.2-2.0 g/kg/day, best met as regular servings of about 0.3 g/kg of high-quality protein after exercise and across the day, usually achievable from food.
used_for: daily protein target and per-meal dose

quote: break point=1.62 (1.03, 2.20) g/kg/day
claim: In resistance-training RCTs, gains in fat-free mass from protein supplementation plateaued at a total protein intake of about 1.6 g/kg/day; the upper 95% confidence limit was 2.2 g/kg/day, which the authors suggest as a target for those wanting to maximise gains.
population: healthy adults in resistance-training RCTs (49 RCTs, mostly young men)
caveat: break point not statistically significant (p=0.079); lean athletes in an energy deficit may need more

quote: Data from 49 studies with 1863 participants showed that dietary protein supplementation significantly (all p<0.05) increased changes (means (95% CI)) in: strength-one-repetition-maximum (2.49 kg (0.64, 4.33)), FFM (0.30 kg (0.09, 0.52))
claim: Adding protein supplements to resistance training produced only modest extra gains: about 2.5 kg more 1RM strength and 0.3 kg more fat-free mass on average.
population: healthy adults in resistance-training RCTs (49 RCTs, 1863 participants)
caveat: effect smaller with increasing age, larger in resistance-trained people; training and total intake matter more than the powder

quote: General recommendations are 0.25 g of a high-quality protein per kg of body weight, or an absolute dose of 20–40 g. ... These protein doses should ideally be evenly distributed, every 3–4 h, across the day.
claim: ISSN: a per-meal protein dose of about 0.25 g/kg (20-40 g) of high-quality protein, spread evenly every 3-4 hours, is the general recommendation.
caveat: per-meal 'ceiling' challenged by Trommelen 2023; total daily intake matters more

quote: we show that the ingestion of 100 g protein results in a greater and more prolonged (>12 h) anabolic response when compared to the ingestion of 25 g protein
claim: In a tracer RCT, 100 g of protein after whole-body resistance exercise produced a larger and longer (>12 h) anabolic response than 25 g, challenging the idea of a per-meal protein ceiling of about 20-25 g.
population: healthy young men (n=12 per group) after one resistance-exercise session
caveat: single acute study measuring protein synthesis, not long-term muscle gain

quote: Our data provide a mechanistic explanation for why larger but less frequent meals are a viable alternative to consuming smaller meals more frequently. A final consideration is that we investigated healthy, young men following a bout of whole-body resistance exercise and do not know if our observations can be extrapolated to other populations and/or conditions.
claim: The authors conclude that fewer, larger protein meals are a viable alternative to frequent smaller ones, but caution that the result may not extend beyond healthy young men.
population: healthy young men after resistance exercise

quote: Resistance training and sufficient protein intake are indispensable mitigators of lean mass loss in a sustained caloric deficit, regardless of the diet type or variant. Total daily protein is of primary importance; specific distribution of the constituent doses is a secondary concern.
claim: ISSN 2026: during an energy deficit, resistance training and enough protein protect lean mass; total daily protein matters most and how it is split across meals is secondary.
population: healthy, physically active or athletic adults in an energy deficit

quote: Daily protein intakes ranging 1.6–2.2 g/kg BW combined with resistance training may optimize muscle anabolism, while higher intakes of 1.9–3.2 g/kg BW can maximize lean mass retention in lean, resistance-trained individuals sustaining hypocaloric conditions.
claim: ISSN 2026: 1.6-2.2 g/kg/day with resistance training may optimise muscle gain; lean, resistance-trained people in an energy deficit may need 1.9-3.2 g/kg/day to keep lean mass.
population: lean, resistance-trained adults; the higher range applies to an energy deficit
caveat: upper range rests on few, short studies in lean trained people; ISSN 2017 gave a similar 2.3-3.1 g/kg/day (NUT-70)

quote: the PROT-AGE study group recommends average daily intake at least in the range of 1.0 to 1.2 g protein per kilogram of body weight per day. Both endurance- and resistance-type exercises are recommended at individualized levels that are safe and tolerated, and higher protein intake (ie, ≥ 1.2 g/kg body weight/d) is advised for those who are exercising and otherwise active.
claim: PROT-AGE: people over 65 should eat at least 1.0-1.2 g protein/kg/day, and at least 1.2 g/kg/day if they exercise or are otherwise active.
caveat: position paper more than 10 years old

quote: Older people with severe kidney disease (ie, estimated GFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m(2)), but who are not on dialysis, are an exception to this rule; these individuals may need to limit protein intake.
claim: Older people with severe kidney disease (eGFR below 30) who are not on dialysis may need to limit protein, so higher-protein advice does not apply to them.
population: older adults with severe chronic kidney disease

quote: Low intensity or skill-based ... 3-5 g/kg of athlete's BW/d ... Moderate exercise program ... 5-7 g/kg/d ... Endurance program (e.g., 1- ... 6-10 g/kg/d ... Extreme commitment (e.g., ... 8-12 g/kg/d ... (e.g., ~1 h/d) ... 3 h/d mod-high-intensity ... > 4-5 h/d mod-high intensity
claim: ACSM/AND/DC daily carbohydrate targets by training load: light, low-intensity or skill-based training 3-5 g/kg/day; moderate programme (about 1 h/day) 5-7 g/kg/day; endurance programme (1-3 h/day moderate-high intensity) 6-10 g/kg/day; extreme commitment (more than 4-5 h/day) 8-12 g/kg/day.
caveat: table text in the PDF is split into columns; pairing of rows checked against the table layout. Targets are for days where training quality matters; on easy days intake can follow energy goals

quote: An additional nutritional strategy for events of >60 minutes duration is to consume carbohydrate according to its potential to enhance performance. ... Typically, an intake of 30 to 60 g/h provides benefits by contributing to muscle fuel needs and maintaining blood glucose concentrations, although in very prolonged events (2.5+ hours) or other scenarios where endogenous carbohydrate stores are substantially depleted, higher intakes (up to 90 g/h) are associated with better performance.
claim: During events longer than 60 minutes, 30-60 g carbohydrate per hour improves performance; in very long events (2.5 h or more) up to 90 g/h is associated with better performance.

quote: At intakes up to 60 g/h, there is no difference between single and multiple transportable carbohydrates, but when intake increases above 60 g/h and the sodium-dependent glucose transporter 1 (SGLT1) becomes saturated, added fructose will result in higher exogenous carbohydrate oxidation rates. ... If single carbohydrate sources are ingested at rates higher than 60 g/h, gastrointestinal problems are likely.
claim: Above about 60 g/h, carbohydrate should come from glucose plus fructose ('multiple transportable carbohydrates'); a single source such as glucose alone above 60 g/h is likely to cause GI problems.

quote: > 90 min of sustained/ intermittent exercise ... Carbohydrate loading ... 36-48 h of 10-12 g/kg BW per 24 h
claim: Carbohydrate loading before events of more than 90 minutes of sustained or intermittent exercise: 10-12 g/kg body weight per day for 36-48 hours.
population: athletes preparing for events longer than 90 min
caveat: table text in the PDF is split into columns; the row pairing was checked against the table layout

quote: Before exercise > 60 min ... 1-4 g/kg consumed 1-4 h before exercise
claim: Before exercise lasting more than 60 minutes, eat 1-4 g/kg of carbohydrate 1-4 hours beforehand, choosing foods that are well tolerated.
population: athletes before sessions or events over 60 min

quote: A carbohydrate intake of ~1.0 to 1.2 g/kg/h, commencing during the early recovery phase and continuing for 4 to 6 hours, will optimize rates of resynthesis of muscle glycogen.
claim: When glycogen must be restored quickly between two fuel-demanding sessions, eat about 1.0-1.2 g/kg/h of carbohydrate starting early in recovery and continuing for 4-6 hours.
population: athletes with short recovery between fuel-demanding sessions
caveat: not needed when there is a full day between sessions; then daily totals matter

quote: runners should aim to consume 150–400 Kcal·h− 1 (carbohydrate, 30–50 g·h− 1; protein, 5–10 g·h− 1) from a variety of calorie-dense foods. Consideration must be given to food palatability, individual tolerance, and the increased preference for savory foods in longer races
claim: ISSN ultra stand: during an ultra-marathon aim for 150-400 kcal per hour (30-50 g carbohydrate and 5-10 g protein per hour) from varied, calorie-dense foods, considering taste, tolerance and the shift towards savoury foods in longer races.
caveat: lower than the up-to-90 g/h of ACSM/AND/DC for events over 2.5 h; evidence is mostly observational

quote: Although current literature advocates CHO ingestion rates up to ~ 90 g·h− 1 for events > 120 min, particularly when using ‘multiple transportable carbohydrates’ containing glucose and fructose [104], such high rates of ingestion may be unrealistic for longer ultra-marathon races (> 6 h). Moreover, this rate of ingestion may lead to nutrient malabsorption and GI distress [105].
claim: ISSN: the up-to-90 g/h carbohydrate guidance for events over 120 min may be unrealistic in ultras longer than 6 hours and can cause malabsorption and GI distress.

quote: Fluid volumes of 450–750 mL·h− 1 (~ 150–250 mL every 20 min) are recommended during racing. To minimize the likelihood of hyponatraemia, electrolytes (mainly sodium) may be needed in concentrations greater than that provided by most commercial products (i.e., > 575 mg·L− 1 sodium).
claim: ISSN ultra stand: drink about 450-750 mL per hour (150-250 mL every 20 min) when racing; sodium above 575 mg per litre of fluid may be needed to reduce hyponatraemia risk, more than most commercial drinks provide.
number: 450-750 mL/h; 150-250 mL every 20 min; >575 mg/L sodium
caveat: needs adjusting to sweat rate, heat and body size; drinking well beyond sweat losses causes hyponatraemia

quote: Moreover, this strategy is considered the most appropriate method of minimizing the risk of hypo- or hyper-hydration during ultra-marathon [16]. However, given that most athletes choose to consume electrolyte formulas by ingesting fluids, drinking-to-thirst may result in the under-consumption of sodium and other vital electrolytes.
claim: In ultras, drinking to thirst is considered the best way to avoid both under- and over-hydration, but because electrolytes usually come in drinks, drinking to thirst alone may supply too little sodium.

quote: Evidence supports progressive gut-training and/or low-FODMAP diets (fermentable oligosaccharide, disaccharide, monosaccharide and polyol) to alleviate symptoms of gastrointestinal distress during racing
claim: Progressive gut training, and in some cases a low-FODMAP diet, can reduce GI distress during ultra racing.
caveat: a low-FODMAP diet is a restrictive therapeutic diet; set it up with a dietitian, not the coach

quote: Therefore, it is important to practice a race nutritional strategy in training and get used to higher volumes of intake or higher carbohydrate intakes.
claim: Practise the race-day eating and drinking plan in training and build up gradually to the volumes and carbohydrate rates planned for the race.
caveat: narrative review partly extrapolated from animal data; the dose and timeline of gut training are not established

quote: The goal of drinking during exercise is to prevent excessive (>2% body weight loss from water deficit) dehydration and excessive changes in electrolyte balance to avert compromised performance.
claim: ACSM: drink during exercise to prevent dehydration beyond 2% of body weight and large electrolyte shifts that impair performance.
caveat: 2007 stand, more than 10 years old; see Goulet 2019 (NUT-35) for evidence that ad libitum drinking performs as well in 1-2 h events

quote: Because there is considerable variability in sweating rates and sweat electrolyte content between individuals, customized fluid replacement programs are recommended. Individual sweat rates can be estimated by measuring body weight before and after exercise.
claim: Sweat rates differ widely between people, so fluid plans should be individual; sweat rate is estimated by weighing before and after exercise.

quote: Athletes may achieve euhydration prior to exercise by consuming a fluid volume equivalent to 5-10 ml/kg BW in the 2 to 4 hours before exercise to achieve urine that is pale yellow in color while allowing for sufficient time for excess fluid to be voided.
claim: Pre-hydration: drink about 5-10 mL/kg body weight in the 2-4 hours before exercise, aiming for pale yellow urine and leaving time to pass the excess.

quote: will typically achieve an intake of 0.4 to 0.8 L/h, ... although this needs to be customized to the athlete’s tolerance and experience, their opportunities for drinking fluids
claim: A typical fluid plan during exercise provides 0.4-0.8 L per hour, customised to tolerance, experience and opportunities to drink.

quote: Sodium should be ingested during exercise when large sweat sodium losses occur. Scenarios include athletes with high sweat rates (> 1.2 L/h), salty sweat, or prolonged exercise exceeding 2 hours in duration.
claim: Take sodium during exercise when sweat sodium losses are large: high sweat rates (above 1.2 L/h), salty sweat, or exercise longer than 2 hours.

quote: effective rehydration requires the intake of a greater volume of fluid (e.g., 125% to 150%) than the final fluid deficit (e.g., 1.25-1.5 L fluid for every 1 kg BW lost).
claim: After exercise, drink about 125-150% of the fluid deficit (1.25-1.5 L per kg body weight lost), with sodium from food or drinks to help retain it.
population: athletes after exercise with a fluid deficit

quote: Over-drinking fluids in excess of sweat and urinary losses is the primary cause of hyponatremia (plasma sodium <135 mmol/L), also known as water intoxication ... Over-hydration is typically seen in recreational athletes since their work outputs and sweat rates are lower than competitive athletes, while their opportunities and belief in the need to drink may be greater.
claim: Drinking more than sweat and urine losses is the main cause of exercise-associated hyponatremia (sodium below 135 mmol/L); it is typically seen in slower recreational athletes, who sweat less and have more chances to drink.
caveat: hyponatremia as an emergency is covered by SAF

quote: The suggested ideal strategy for exercise performance advises limiting body mass losses to less than 2% throughout activity but not gaining weight during exercise.
claim: NATA: limit body mass loss during activity to less than 2%, and never gain weight during exercise (weight gain means over-drinking).

quote: If athletes do not know their individual sweat rates, drinking to thirst during activity most likely represents a safe strategy to prevent overdrinking.
claim: If an athlete's sweat rate is unknown, drinking to thirst is a safe default to avoid over-drinking.

quote: Thirst may be delayed, so for competitive athletes striving to maximize performance, using a “drink when thirsty” strategy may compromise performance.
claim: For competitive athletes chasing performance, thirst may lag behind needs, so a planned strategy based on known sweat rate may be better than drinking to thirst.

quote: As a general rule, those participating in physical activity lasting less than 1 hour should require no substances other than water.
claim: For activity lasting less than 1 hour, water alone is enough.

quote: Mean change in body mass for the PD and ALD conditions was - 1.0 ± 0.5% and - 2.1 ± 0.7%, respectively. Compared with PD, ALD improved EP by 0.98 ± 0.44% (95% confidence interval 0.11-1.84%). The greater EP conferred by ALD is likely trivial.
claim: Meta-analysis: in 1-2 h cycling or running in temperate to warm conditions, ad libitum drinking (about 2.1% body mass loss) performed as well as programmed drinking (about 1.0% loss); the small advantage for ad libitum drinking was likely trivial.
population: endurance-trained participants, exercise 1-2 h, 28 degrees C on average (7 studies, 82 subjects)
caveat: small evidence base; does not cover events longer than about 2 h or hot ultras

quote: identifying a syndrome of deleterious health and performance outcomes experienced by female and male athletes exposed to low energy availability (LEA; inadequate energy intake in relation to exercise energy expenditure)
claim: IOC 2023: REDs is a syndrome of harmful health and performance outcomes in female and male athletes exposed to low energy availability, meaning too little energy intake for the exercise energy expended.

quote: The concept of the LEA threshold (30 kcal/kg FFM/day), below which health problems occurred, was based on elegant but short-term laboratory studies that investigated stepwise changes in EA, perturbations of sex hormones ... in a small sample of sedentary females.
claim: The 30 kcal/kg FFM/day low-energy-availability threshold came from short laboratory studies in a small sample of sedentary women.
population: origin: sedentary women in short laboratory studies

quote: Therefore, although EA calculations may inform research interventions or observations, there are risks in setting a definitive clinical threshold of EA due to many moderating factors.
claim: IOC 2023: energy availability calculations can inform research, but setting a definitive clinical threshold is risky because many factors modify individual responses.
caveat: measuring energy availability in free-living athletes is burdensome and error-prone

quote: where an EA of 45 kcal/kg FFM/d was found to be associated with energy balance and optimal health; meanwhile, a chronic reduction in EA, (particularly below 30 kcal/kg FFM/d) was associated with impairments of a variety of body functions.
claim: ACSM/AND/DC 2016 (older view): energy availability of 45 kcal/kg FFM/day is associated with energy balance and health, and chronic values below 30 kcal/kg FFM/day with impaired body functions.
caveat: IOC 2023 warns against using these as fixed clinical cut-offs

quote: Many sports have engrained cultures where coaches and members of the athlete health and performance team exert subtle to extreme pressure on athletes to regulate body weight and composition.
claim: Coaches and support staff in many sports put subtle to extreme pressure on athletes to regulate body weight and composition.

quote: In athletic populations sustaining hypocaloric conditions, limiting weekly rates of weight loss to 0.5%–1.0% of total body weight may optimize the retention of lean mass
claim: For athletes in an energy deficit, limiting weight loss to 0.5-1.0% of body weight per week may best preserve lean mass.
population: athletic adults in an energy deficit

quote: Another trial in this context by Garthe et al. [53] compared the effects of slow (0.7% per week) versus fast (1.4% per week) weight loss in elite athletes in a mix of sports. The results indicated that fat mass decreased to a statistically similar magnitude in both groups, but lean mass increased in the slow weight loss condition, and remained unchanged in the fast weight loss condition.
claim: Citing Garthe 2011 (single RCT): elite athletes losing 0.7% of body weight per week lost similar fat but gained lean mass, whereas those losing 1.4% per week did not gain lean mass.
population: elite athletes in mixed sports doing resistance training (single RCT)
caveat: one small RCT; supports, but does not prove, a slower rate

quote: intake by ~250 to 500 kcal/d from their periodized energy needs, while either maintaining or slightly increasing energy expenditure, can achieve progress towards short-term body composition goals over approximately 3 to 6 weeks.
claim: ACSM/AND/DC: for most athletes a reduction of about 250-500 kcal/day from periodised energy needs, with stable or slightly higher expenditure, achieves short-term body-composition goals over about 3-6 weeks.

quote: Very-low-energy diets (<800 kcal/day) and low-energy diets (800–1200 kcal/day) produce greater short-term weight loss but lack long-term advantages over less aggressive energy restrictions, ... These aggressive diets may increase lean mass loss, ... Caution is warranted about insufficiencies in vitamins, minerals, fiber, and other nutrients.
claim: ISSN 2026: very-low-energy (<800 kcal/day) and low-energy (800-1200 kcal/day) diets give faster short-term loss but no long-term advantage over moderate restriction, and may increase lean mass loss and nutrient shortfalls.
population: adults, mostly from clinical research in overweight and obesity

quote: Consider low-energy diets (800 to 1,200 kilocalories per day, also known as low-calorie diets) only as part of a multicomponent overweight and obesity management strategy with long-term support within a specialist overweight and obesity management service ... for people: living with obesity (with or without diabetes) or living with overweight and with type 2 diabetes.
claim: NICE: consider low-energy diets of 800-1,200 kcal/day only within a specialist overweight and obesity service with long-term support, for people living with obesity (or overweight with type 2 diabetes).
population: adults living with obesity, or overweight with type 2 diabetes (UK clinical guideline)
used_for: crash diets: why the coach refers

quote: Consider very-low-energy diets (under 800 kilocalories per day, also known as very-low-calorie diets) only as part of a multicomponent strategy within a specialist overweight and obesity management service, for people who: are living with obesity and have a clinically assessed need to lose weight rapidly
claim: NICE: very-low-energy diets (under 800 kcal/day) only within a specialist service for people with obesity and a clinically assessed need to lose weight rapidly.
used_for: crash diets: why the coach refers

quote: Do not use low-energy diets or very-low-energy diets as a long-term strategy to manage obesity. ... Ensure that low-energy and very-low-energy diets: are nutritionally complete last no more than 12 weeks include ongoing clinical support and supervision
claim: NICE: low-energy and very-low-energy diets must be nutritionally complete, last no more than 12 weeks and include ongoing clinical support and supervision; they are not a long-term strategy.
used_for: crash diets: why the coach refers

quote: Advise people not to use restrictive diets that are nutritionally unbalanced, because they are ineffective in the long term and can be harmful.
claim: NICE: advise people not to use nutritionally unbalanced restrictive diets, because they are ineffective in the long term and can be harmful.
used_for: crash diets: why the coach declines

quote: Ensure that any dietary approaches that maintain an energy deficit are offered with support (for example by an appropriately trained healthcare professional such as a Registered dietitian or registered nutritionist)
claim: NICE: any diet that maintains an energy deficit should come with support, for example from a registered dietitian or registered nutritionist.

quote: Supplements claiming to directly or indirectly enhance performance are typically the largest group of products marketed to athletes, but only a few (including caffeine, creatine, specific buffering agents and nitrate) have good evidence of benefits.
claim: IOC 2018: of the many performance supplements on the market, only a few (caffeine, creatine, specific buffering agents and nitrate) have good evidence of benefit.
caveat: responses vary between individuals and scenarios; trial in training before competition

quote: A complete nutritional assessment should be undertaken before decisions regarding supplement use are made.
claim: IOC 2018: a complete nutritional assessment should come before any decision to use supplements.

quote: Although the original study reported that ~15% of more than 600 products acquired from around the world contained undeclared prohormones
claim: Contamination is a real anti-doping and health risk: in the original survey about 15% of over 600 supplements contained undeclared prohormones.
caveat: samples were not random, so the true prevalence is uncertain

quote: Various efforts are being made to address the problems, including the use of third-party auditing activities to identify products that athletes may consider to be at ‘low risk’ of containing prohibited substances. There can be no absolute guarantee that any product is entirely safe, but these schemes do help the athlete to manage the risk.
claim: Third-party testing schemes help manage, but cannot eliminate, the risk of prohibited substances in supplements.
population: athletes, especially those subject to anti-doping rules

quote: Several measures performed simultaneously provide the best assessment and determine the stage of deficiency. ... Athletes with iron deficiency require clinical follow-up ... High-dose iron supplements, however, should not be taken unless iron deficiency is present.
claim: Do not take high-dose iron supplements unless iron deficiency has been diagnosed; iron status needs several blood measures taken together, and athletes with iron deficiency need clinical follow-up.
caveat: the same table notes that iron in people with adequate stores can cause GI symptoms and, in the extreme, haemochromatosis and liver failure

quote: Caffeine has consistently been shown to improve exercise performance when consumed in doses of 3–6 mg/kg body mass. Minimal effective doses of caffeine currently remain unclear but they may be as low as 2 mg/kg body mass. Very high doses of caffeine (e.g. 9 mg/kg) are associated with a high incidence of side-effects ... The most commonly used timing of caffeine supplementation is 60 min pre-exercise.
claim: ISSN: caffeine at 3-6 mg/kg body mass (commonly about 60 min before exercise) consistently improves performance; doses as low as 2 mg/kg may work, and very high doses such as 9 mg/kg cause frequent side effects without extra benefit.
caveat: sleep disruption and anxiety vary between individuals; position stand addresses adults

quote: The quickest method of increasing muscle creatine stores may be to consume ~0.3 g/kg/day of creatine monohydrate for 5–7-days followed by 3–5 g/day thereafter to maintain elevated stores. Initially, ingesting smaller amounts of creatine monohydrate (e.g., 3–5 g/day) will increase muscle creatine stores over a 3–4 week period
claim: ISSN: creatine monohydrate either loaded at about 0.3 g/kg/day for 5-7 days then 3-5 g/day, or simply 3-5 g/day, which saturates muscle stores over 3-4 weeks.

quote: There is no compelling scientific evidence that the short- or long-term use of creatine monohydrate (up to 30 g/day for 5 years) has any detrimental effects on otherwise healthy individuals
claim: ISSN: no compelling evidence that creatine monohydrate (up to 30 g/day for up to 5 years) harms otherwise healthy people.
caveat: ISSN authors declare creatine-industry funding and consulting

quote: initial studies reported that creatine loading promoted a short-term fluid retention (e.g., about 0.5 – 1.0 L) that was generally proportional to the acute weight gain observed
claim: Creatine loading causes short-term fluid retention of about 0.5-1.0 L, roughly matching the acute weight gain.

quote: In general, vitamin and mineral supplements are unnecessary for the athlete who consumes a diet providing high-energy availability from a variety of nutrient-dense foods. ... targeted supplementation may be indicated to treat or prevent deficiency (e.g., iron, vitamin D).
claim: Vitamin and mineral supplements are generally unnecessary for athletes eating enough energy from varied, nutrient-dense foods; targeted supplements (for example iron or vitamin D) are for diagnosed or likely deficiency.

quote: the adolescent athlete should be encouraged to moderate eating patterns to reflect daily exercise demands and provide a regular spread of high quality carbohydrate and protein sources over the day, especially in the period immediately after training. SDA recommends that consideration also be given to the dietary calcium, Vitamin D and iron intake of adolescent athletes due to the elevated risk of deficiency of these nutrients.
claim: Sports Dietitians Australia: adolescent athletes should match eating to daily training, spread quality carbohydrate and protein over the day (especially right after training) and watch calcium, vitamin D and iron intake.

quote: it is the position of SDA that nutrient needs should be met by core foods rather than supplements, as the recommendation of dietary supplements to developing athletes over-emphasizes their ability to manipulate performance in comparison with other training and dietary strategies.
claim: Sports Dietitians Australia: adolescent athletes should meet nutrient needs from core foods, not supplements.

quote: Provided adequate energy is being consumed, ... Protein intake at ~ 0.11 g/kg/h during post-exercise recovery, or the equivalent of ~ 1.5 g/kg/day (e.g. ~ 0.3 g protein/kg × 5 meal times), should be sufficient to replace any exercise-induced amino acid oxidative losses, enhance whole body net protein balance, and support the normal growth and development of adolescent athletes
claim: About 1.5 g protein/kg/day (for example about 0.3 g/kg at 5 eating occasions) should be sufficient for adolescent athletes, provided total energy intake is adequate.
caveat: narrative review; energy intake adequate is the precondition

quote: Generally, it is considered inappropriate for young athletes to be encouraged to consume dietary supplements for performance enhancement. This view is consistent with those of leading sporting organisations and expert groups [90–92]. This recommendation excludes the clinical use of dietary supplements (e.g., calcium, iron, vitamin D) when taken under appropriate guidance from suitably qualified health professionals
claim: Young athletes should not be encouraged to use performance supplements; clinical supplements (calcium, iron, vitamin D) are for use under a doctor's or sports dietitian's guidance.

quote: However, we recommend that creatine supplementation only be considered for use by younger athletes who: a.) are involved in serious/competitive supervised training; b.) are consuming a well-balanced and performance enhancing diet; c.) are knowledgeable about appropriate use of creatine; and d.) do not exceed recommended dosages.
claim: ISSN (minority view): creatine may be considered for younger athletes only if they train seriously under supervision, eat a balanced diet, understand appropriate use and stay within recommended doses.
caveat: conflicts with Sports Dietitians Australia and the paediatric view covered by POP; authors have industry ties

quote: Athletes should be referred to a registered dietitian/nutritionist for a personalized nutrition plan.
claim: ACSM/AND/DC: refer athletes to a registered dietitian/nutritionist for a personalised nutrition plan.

quote: Medical nutritional therapeutic advice pertaining to unique dietary considerations (eating disorders, food allergies, diabetes, gastrointestinal issues, etc.)
claim: Medical nutrition therapy, such as advice for eating disorders, food allergies, diabetes or gastrointestinal problems, is listed as a sports dietitian role.

quote: A ketogenic diet has largely neutral or detrimental effects on athletic performance compared to a diet higher in carbohydrates and lower in fat, despite achieving significantly elevated levels of fat oxidation during exercise (~1.5 g/min).
claim: ISSN 2024: a ketogenic diet raises fat oxidation (about 1.5 g/min) but has largely neutral or detrimental effects on performance compared with higher-carbohydrate diets.

quote: All studies involving elite athletes showed a performance decrement from a ketogenic diet, all lasting six weeks or less. Of the two studies lasting more than six weeks, only one reported a statistically significant benefit of a ketogenic diet.
claim: In elite athletes every study (all up to six weeks) found worse performance on a ketogenic diet; of two longer studies only one found a benefit, so long-term adaptation remains debated.
caveat: includes Burke 2017 (elite race walkers): ketogenic diet reduced exercise economy and removed the training benefit

quote: Vegetarian athletes may be at risk for low intakes of energy, protein, fat, creatine, carnosine, n-3 fatty acids, and key micronutrients such as iron, calcium, riboflavin, zinc, and vitamin B12.
claim: Vegetarian (and by extension vegan) athletes may be at risk of low intakes of energy, protein, creatine, n-3 fatty acids, iron, calcium, zinc and vitamin B12.

quote: Higher protein intakes (2.3–3.1 g/kg/d) may be needed to maximize the retention of lean body mass in resistance-trained subjects during hypocaloric periods.
claim: ISSN 2017: resistance-trained people in an energy deficit may need 2.3-3.1 g/kg/day of protein to maximise lean-mass retention.
population: resistance-trained adults in an energy deficit

quote: A complete assessment should ideally include a detailed medical and nutritional history, diet evaluation, anthropometry and body composition analysis, and biochemical testing. ... is not at risk for health issues associated with supplement use, including interactions with prescription or over-the-counter medications
claim: IOC 2018: the nutritional assessment before supplementation includes medical history and biochemical testing and must check for interactions with prescription or over-the-counter medicines.

quote: If rapid restoration of glycogen is required (< 4 h of recovery time) then the following strategies should be considered:aggressive carbohydrate refeeding (1.2 g/kg/h)
claim: ISSN: when glycogen must be restored in under 4 h, aggressive carbohydrate refeeding at about 1.2 g/kg/h is a strategy to consider.
population: healthy exercising adults, mainly highly trained
caveat: Matters only when sessions are less than 4 h apart; with a full day between sessions daily totals matter instead.

quote: Meeting the total daily intake of protein, preferably with evenly spaced protein feedings (approximately every 3 h during the day), should be viewed as a primary area of emphasis for exercising individuals.
claim: ISSN: meeting total daily protein intake, preferably in evenly spaced feedings about every 3 h, is the primary area of emphasis for people who exercise.
population: healthy exercising adults, mainly highly trained

quote: Post-exercise ingestion (immediately to 2-h post) of high-quality protein sources stimulates robust increases in MPS.
claim: ISSN: protein of high quality eaten from immediately to 2 h after exercise stimulates robust increases in muscle protein synthesis.
population: healthy exercising adults, mainly highly trained
caveat: Muscle protein synthesis is a short-term marker, not proof of better long-term gains; total daily protein matters more (NUT-73).

quote: Circumstances where planned drinking is optimal include longer duration activities of > 90 min, particularly in the heat; higher-intensity exercise with high sweat rates; exercise where performance is a concern; and when carbohydrate intake of 1 g/min is desired.
claim: Planned drinking is optimal for activities longer than 90 min (especially in the heat), higher-intensity exercise with high sweat rates, when performance is a concern, and when carbohydrate intake of 1 g/min is wanted.
caveat: Narrative review; 1 g/min equals 60 g/h of carbohydrate.

quote: Circumstances where drinking to thirst may be sufficient include short duration exercise of < 1 h to 90 min; exercise in cooler conditions; and lower-intensity exercise. It is recommended to never drink so much that weight is gained.
claim: Drinking to thirst may be sufficient for short exercise (under 1 h to 90 min), cooler conditions and lower intensity; never drink so much that body weight rises.
used_for: when drinking to thirst is enough
caveat: Narrative review.

quote: Individuals with high sweat rates and/or those concerned with exercise performance should determine sweat rates under conditions (exercise intensity, pace) and environments similar to that anticipated when competing and tailor drinking to prevent body mass losses > 2%.
claim: People with high sweat rates or performance concerns should measure sweat rate in conditions like competition and tailor drinking to prevent body mass loss above 2%.
population: exercising adults with high sweat rates or performance goals
caveat: Narrative review.

quote: This included the sufficiency of energy and protein; the adequacy of vitamin B12, iron, zinc, calcium, iodine and vitamin D; and the lack of the long-chain n-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA in most plant-based sources.
claim: Vegan diets need attention to energy and protein sufficiency, vitamin B12, iron, zinc, calcium, iodine and vitamin D, and to the lack of EPA and DHA in most plant foods.
caveat: Narrative review with little vegan-athlete data.

quote: via the strategic management of food and appropriate supplementation, it is the contention of this article that a nutritive vegan diet can be designed to achieve the dietary needs of most athletes satisfactorily.
claim: The author argues that with strategic food choices and appropriate supplementation, a vegan diet can meet the needs of most athletes.
used_for: vegan diet is workable, do not discourage
caveat: Expert opinion; the article says empirical research in athletic vegans is lacking.

quote: Increase protein to 1.7–2.0 g ∙ kg−1 and up to 1.8–2.7 g ∙ kg−1 during weight loss phases (obtain from range of plant-based foods).
claim: The review's table suggests vegan athletes raise protein to 1.7-2.0 g/kg and up to 1.8-2.7 g/kg during weight-loss phases, from a range of plant foods.
caveat: Expert opinion from a narrative review, set above the usual 1.4-2.0 g/kg (NUT-01) because plant protein is less digestible; no trial in vegan athletes sets this figure.

quote: for healthy older people, the diet should provide at least 1.0-1.2 g protein/kg body weight/day
claim: ESPEN: healthy older people should eat at least 1.0-1.2 g protein/kg body weight/day.
caveat: Agrees with PROT-AGE (NUT-10).

quote: for older people who are malnourished or at risk of malnutrition because they have acute or chronic illness, the diet should provide 1.2-1.5 g protein/kg body weight/day, with even higher intake for individuals with severe illness or injury
claim: ESPEN: older people who are malnourished or at risk because of acute or chronic illness should eat 1.2-1.5 g protein/kg/day, and more with severe illness or injury.
population: older people who are malnourished or ill
used_for: refer ill or malnourished older clients
caveat: A clinical nutrition decision for a doctor or dietitian, not a coach.

quote: daily physical activity or exercise (resistance training, aerobic exercise) should be undertaken by all older people, for as long as possible
claim: ESPEN: all older people should do daily physical activity or exercise, resistance and aerobic, for as long as possible.
caveat: Dose details are in the POP cluster.
